title: Neural Networks Intro
subtitle: Building Blocks of Deep Learning
content:
🧠 Biological Inspiration

Note: ANNs are loosely inspired by but not modeled on biological neurons. The brain has ~86 billion neurons with complex chemistry; ANNs use much simpler mathematical units and are a useful computational tool, not a brain model.

Scale varies widely: Small demos have a few hundred parameters; modern LLMs have billions. Parameter count is not directly comparable to neuron count.

🔧 Perceptrons

Formula: Output = f(Σ(wᵢ·xᵢ) + b)

Components: Inputs, Weights, Weighted Sum, Activation Function, Output

📈 Activation Functions

FunctionFormulaUse
ReLUmax(0, x)Hidden layers
Sigmoid1/(1+e^-x)Binary output
Softmaxe^xᵢ/Σe^xʲMulti-class output
LinearxRegression output

Why Non-Linearity? Without it, deep networks = single-layer networks!

🏗️ Network Architecture

Input Layer: Receives data

Hidden Layers: Learn feature representations

Output Layer: Produces predictions

Standard Flow: Input → Hidden → Hidden → ... → Output

🔄 Forward & Backward Propagation

Forward: Calculate output from input

Backward (Backprop): Update weights based on error

Learning Rate: Controls weight update size

⚙️ Optimizers: from SGD to AdamW

Backprop computes the gradient. The optimizer decides how the weights actually move.

  • SGD: w -= lr * grad. The simplest. Slow to navigate ravines and saddle points; oscillates in narrow directions.
  • Momentum: keep a running average of past gradients and use it as a "velocity". Smooths out oscillations and speeds up consistent directions. v = beta * v + grad; w -= lr * v.
  • AdaGrad / RMSProp: scale the per-parameter learning rate by a running estimate of the gradient's magnitude. Big steps on rarely-updating params, small steps on fast-changing ones.
  • Adam: momentum + per-parameter adaptive scaling. The default first-choice optimizer for most modern deep learning. beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, lr=1e-3 is a good starting point.
  • AdamW: Adam with decoupled weight decay (not the same as L2 reg via Adam!). Default for transformer fine-tuning; better generalization than Adam in practice.

Rule of thumb: Adam (or AdamW) at lr=1e-3 first. If training is unstable or noisy, dial lr down to 3e-4 or 5e-4. For LLM fine-tuning use 1e-5 to 2e-4 (much lower, see Lesson 14 Fine-tuning & PEFT).

🛡️ Regularization: Fighting Overfitting

Without regularization, a deep network can memorize the training set. Five common defenses:

  • Dropout: randomly zero a fraction of activations during training (typical 0.1-0.5). Forces redundancy; the network can't rely on any single neuron. Disabled at inference.
  • L1 / L2 weight decay: add a penalty on the size of the weights to the loss. L1 pushes small weights to zero (sparsity, feature selection). L2 (weight decay) shrinks all weights gently. AdamW implements L2-style decay correctly.
  • Batch normalization: normalize each layer's activations to mean 0 / var 1, then learn scale and shift. Stabilizes and speeds training; reduces sensitivity to LR.
  • LayerNorm: the transformer-friendly variant - normalize per sample across features (not across the batch). Used everywhere inside modern transformers.
  • Early stopping: monitor a validation metric; stop (and revert to best) when it stops improving for N epochs. The cheapest, most universal regularizer.

Diagnostic: if train loss keeps dropping but val loss turns upward, you're overfitting - add dropout, weight decay, or early stopping. If both losses plateau high, you're underfitting - reduce regularization, train longer, or use a bigger model.

🧪 Spot-the-Overfit Checklist

  • Train acc much higher than val acc (gap > 10 points)
  • Train loss still decreasing but val loss starts increasing
  • Model performs very differently on different random seeds - high variance
  • Performance drops sharply when you remove a few training examples - the model memorized them

One or more of these? Reaction: dropout, weight decay, early stopping, more data (or augmentation).

💪 Why Deep Learning?

  • Automatic Feature Learning: No manual feature engineering
  • Hierarchical Representations: Low-level → high-level features
  • Scalability: Improves with more data and compute
  • Versatility: Works for images, text, audio, etc.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an activation function?

options.text: Introduce non-linearity (without it, deep networks collapse to a single linear layer)

questions.explanation: Activation functions introduce non-linearity. Without them, stacking layers is mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer, so depth adds nothing.

questions.question: Which activation function is most commonly used in hidden layers?
questions.explanation: ReLU is the default for hidden layers - cheap to compute, doesn't saturate for positive inputs, and trains well.

questions.question: What does the backpropagation algorithm do?

options.text: Computes gradients of the loss w.r.t. every weight using the chain rule

questions.explanation: Backprop applies the chain rule layer-by-layer from the loss backward, giving gradients used by the optimizer to update weights.

questions.question: If you remove all non-linearities from a 100-layer network, what is it equivalent to?

options.text: A single linear layer (composition of linear maps is linear)

questions.explanation: Without nonlinear activations, the composition of matrices is just another matrix, so depth provides no extra expressiveness. This is why non-linearity is essential.

questions.question: Softmax converts logits z into probabilities. What range are its outputs in and what do they sum to?

options.text: Each output in (0,1); they sum to 1
Each output in [-1, 1]; they sum to 0
Each output in [0, infinity); they sum to 1
Each output is unbounded; they sum to whatever

questions.explanation: Softmax exponentiates and normalizes; outputs are valid probabilities in (0,1) summing to 1. This makes it the standard output for classification.
